Instead of writing about the "intelligence" behind it, I built a working version of an extractive logic. Upload a photo and it reads it the way the camera would: a 5-zone tone curve (blacks, shadows, midtones, highlights, whites), real white balance/temperature, exposure, contrast, dynamic range, and grain, all pulled from the actual pixels, no presets. From that, it generates three things: a "developed pattern," an abstract, textile-looking pattern built from the photo's own real colors and tones, so it's basically a visual fingerprint of the image; a vintage-style recipe receipt that translates the readout into plain language plus the full technical settings; and a recipe chart with a pie chart of the tone zones and sliding gauges for saturation and warm/cool temp. The whole site is styled like an old-school desktop: beveled windows, pixel cursor, draggable pop-ups, so the camera's invisible math feels tactile instead of hidden in a menu. You can save recipes to 'the collection' and pull them back up later with the original photo, pattern, and receipt all together. Basically: making the camera show its work.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
keep me company. runs on the logic ELIZA used in 1966: classify what comes in, match it to a scripted line, nothing more. Borrowed directly: input is sorted into a handful of categories, each mapped to a pool of pre-written responses, the way ELIZA matched keywords to transformation rules. 
What's added: no parsing of meaning at all, and a hidden mood value — continuous, cumulative, quietly decaying — that ELIZA never had, giving the page something closer to a memory. The question underneath it: if something responds to everything you do, every time, without ever understanding any of it, is that companionship — or a very convincing imitation of one?
What did you learn from making this? (ma: This project taught me that the illusion of intelligence doesn't require intelligence at all. Before this, whenever I imagined building something that felt responsive or alive, I reached straight for a large language model — I'd never seriously considered any other way to fake understanding. Working within ELIZA's constraints forced me to think differently: keyword matching, weighted randomness, and a simple decaying mood value turned out to be enough to make a response feel personal. I learned that presence is often mistaken for comprehension, and that limitation, not complexity, is what makes a system's behavior feel intentional and alive.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
“Are You Human Enough?” is an interactive CAPTCHA project that explores how digital systems represent and classify human behavior. The project contains three versions of the same verification experience. V1 makes the mechanism visible through mouse tracking, activity logs, risk scoring, and behavioral feedback. V2 hides most of this information and presents a quieter interface, asking users to trust an unseen system. V3 sits between them: it observes typing behavior and offers short comments without revealing the complete formula.
By comparing these interfaces, the project investigates how visual design and feedback influence people’s perception of technological intelligence. The system does not truly understand whether someone is human. It translates actions—such as speed, accuracy, cursor movement, and corrections—into data and applies predefined rules. The interactive homepage connects the three experiments through draggable CAPTCHA images that move, collide, resize, and transform.

Week 1 — System Research
Research mapping how CAPTCHA systems translate human behavior into data, risk scores, and classifications.
File 2 description:
Week 2 — Testing and Observations
Three interaction tests compare how speed, accuracy, and cursor movement produce human, uncertain, or bot-like results.
File 3 description:
Week 3 — Interface Comparison
A comparison of three CAPTCHA interfaces that reveal, partially reveal, or hide how the system observes and judges users.

What did you learn from making this? (ma:
I learned that an interface strongly affects how intelligent, trustworthy, or threatening a system appears. Even when different versions use similar rule-based logic, exposing tracking data makes the system feel more invasive, while hiding the mechanism can make it seem smoother but also more mysterious.
Building the project also showed me that behavioral data is never neutral. A fast response, limited mouse movement, keyboard navigation, or repeated correction can be interpreted as suspicious even when it comes from a real person. These classifications depend on assumptions about what “normal” human behavior should look like.
Technically, I learned how to collect interaction data locally, visualize mouse movement, create explainable scoring rules, manage responsive interfaces, and design playful drag-and-collision interactions. Most importantly, I learned that systems do not simply recognize users—they construct representations of them from incomplete traces.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
Find the Day is an interactive prototype that explores how a personal experience is translated into a specific date that a computational system can understand.
The project began with my analysis of Days Matter, a date-tracking app that counts down to future events and counts up from past ones. I became interested not in how the app calculates time, but in an earlier and less visible step: before a system can calculate or remind us about a date, a personal experience first has to be converted into structured temporal information.
In the final prototype, the interface takes the form of a personal calendar. If the user already knows when an experience happened, they can add the date directly. If they remember the experience but cannot place it precisely in time, they can enter a “Find the Day” process. An anonymous account asks questions about temporal clues such as season, weather, clothing, weekdays. As the user answers, a calendar updates in real time and gradually narrows the possible date range.
The system distinguishes between dates that are clearly remembered, dates that are inferred or selected, and experiences that cannot reasonably be reduced to a single day. Rather than treating every result as equally certain, the prototype makes uncertainty part of the output.
Through this project, I use date reconstruction as a way to examine a broader question: before a system can appear intelligent, what kinds of human experience must first be translated into information that the system can recognize and process?
File 1 description: Final presentation documenting the development of my project from the initial analysis of Days Matter to the final “Find the Day” prototype, including the reconstruction process, two interface experiments, playtest observations, and final reflection on uncertainty and perceived intelligence.
File 2 description: Screen recording of the final “Find the Day” prototype. The video demonstrates how a user moves from an uncertain memory to a specific date through conversation with an anonymous account.
File 3 description: Decision tree from the early development of the project. This diagram maps how a personal experience is translated into a date a system can process, and shows the three possible outcomes: Exact Date, Selected Date, or Cannot Be Represented.
Credit (List out collaborators, tutorial: Tegmark, Max. Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. Chapter 2, Days Matter app, p5.js, GitHub Pages, Chatgpt, Claude
Anyone's work inspired you at the open c: Yes. I was inspired by several projects, especially the different ways people interpreted and visualized intelligence through interaction.
What did you learn from making this? (ma:
At the beginning of this project, I associated “intelligence” with the system’s ability to remember and calculate. Days Matter could remember a birthday that I might forget, calculate how far away it was, and prompt me to take action. This initially made the system feel intelligent.
Reconstructing the system changed my understanding of where that intelligence comes from. I realized that before a system can calculate anything, the user has already done a large amount of interpretive work. A complex personal experience has to be named, categorized, and often reduced to a single date before the system can process it.
This became especially clear when I tested ambiguous memories. Some experiences do not naturally belong to one exact moment. To make them computationally legible, the user may have to infer, approximate, or manually choose a date. Once entered into the calendar, however, that selected date can appear just as precise as a date that was known from the beginning.
The playtests also showed me that the presentation of a system strongly affects how its behavior is interpreted. When I exposed the decision tree, people understood the logic more clearly. When I hid the same rules inside a conversation, the system could feel more human-like or analytical. In the final version, I tried to combine these two qualities by making the narrowing date range visible while keeping some of the filtering logic hidden.
The most important thing I learned is that intelligent behavior is not only about producing an answer. It is also about representing the limits of what a system knows. Sometimes a system should distinguish between what is known, what is inferred, and what cannot be resolved, rather than converting uncertainty into a falsely precise result.

Let Me See is an experimental OCR prototype that explores the difference between reading, recognizing, and understanding.
The system compares an image with reference characters and gives a result based on visual similarity. But reading involves more than recognizing a letter; it also involves understanding and interpreting meaning. Instead of simply showing an answer, the machine hesitates, uses humor, and asks the user for feedback. These simple behaviors can make a basic pattern-matching process feel more human and more complex than it actually is.

What did you learn from making this? (ma:
I realized that even simple things like hesitation and humor can make a machine seem more human. They can also make a simple process feel more complex than it actually is.
What I learned most clearly is that reading and understanding are not the same thing. When we read, we do more than recognize letters. We understand and interpret their meaning.
My prototype only compares visual patterns and recognizes characters. But through language, hesitation, and interaction, it can seem as if the machine is actually thinking.
This made me realize that how a machine speaks changes how we see it. The machine did not become more intelligent. What changed was our perception of what it was doing.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
Did the Gods Say That is an interactive project inspired by Jiaobei, a traditional Chinese divination practice in which people throw two crescent-shaped blocks to seek answers from the gods. The project began with my interest in rainmaking rituals and gradually developed into an exploration of how people interpret responses from a system they cannot fully understand.

I first recreated the basic logic of Jiaobei as a digital system, then added randomness, delays, subtle changes in language, and reactions to repeated questions. Although the system does not actually understand what the user is asking, these small forms of feedback can make it appear as if it is thinking, hesitating, or even becoming annoyed. Through this process, the project explores how easily people can assign intention and meaning to uncertain responses, especially when the mechanism behind them is not completely visible.

What did you learn from making this? (ma:
Through this project, I learned that people do not simply accept the responses given by a system. When the mechanism is completely hidden, they often try to understand or reverse-engineer its logic. However, when I added small details such as delays, changing responses, and reactions to repeated questions, the system began to feel more human even though it still did not understand the questions.

This made me realize that very simple feedback can strongly influence how people interpret a system. We may begin to see hesitation, emotion, or intention in something that is actually based on simple rules and randomness. In a way, this helped me understand why uncertain signs can become meaningful when people are actively looking for an answer.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
This is a research project exploring how "intelligence" can be perceived in systems by unique structures and systems. The specific claim being tested is "Intelligence is when a system evokes fear and stress". 

The core of the system is taken from a card game called "Flip 7". It is a probability-based game where a deck of cards numbered 1 to 12 (their value), with a distribution scaled based on the value (one 1, two 2s, three 3s, up to twelve 12s), is drawn one at a time. If you draw a card that's already in your collection, you die ("consumed"). If it's new, you score safely. You can "feed" (draw) or "flee" (bank your score).

In The Beast, by completely hiding numerical data, percentages, and rigid rules, the system forces the human operator to make decisions based on sensory overload and biological instinct rather than rational calculation. The system appears to "feel" angry and "decide" to attack, but it is merely executing a standard Boolean logic check. The interface weaponizes the unknown, proving that a UI can act as a psychological manipulator, transforming a static probability curve into the illusion of an autonomous predator.

Color Studio is an interactive website that helps people explore their personal colors through a photograph. It automatically samples skin, hair, and eye colors, then suggests a seasonal palette with 34 colors and matching accessories.
The project developed through four assignments: mapping personal color analysis, reconstructing a contrast calculation, creating two interfaces for the same rule, and combining these ideas into a working website. One interface showed the calculations, while the other presented the result as a personal interpretation.
The project asks how a system turns appearance into data—and how its design makes that interpretation feel intelligent and trustworthy.

What did you learn from making this? (ma:
Creating two interfaces helped me understand how the same calculation can be presented as either a simple measurement or a personal judgment. A polished design and confident wording can make an answer seem more certain than it is.
My main takeaway is that a useful system should explain its limits and give people room to explore, rather than present a suggestion as a final truth.
